title: The Line and the Sea: Aéropostale, Patagonia, and the Flight That Did Not Return
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Lyon, rue du Peyrat, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a family apartment on the rue du Peyrat, in Lyon's second arrondissement, a third child is born to Viscount Jean de Saint-Exupéry and Marie Boyer de Fonscolombe. The name is old and the money is not. Four years later the father dies of a stroke, and the widow takes the five children on a circuit of relatives' houses in the Ain and the Var. The title outlasts the income. What the boy learns first, before any of the rest of it, is how to live in rooms that belong to somebody else and to leave them when the visit ends.
suggested_refs: The birth apartment on the rue du Peyrat, Lyon second arrondissement

stops.name: Saint-Maurice-de-Rémens, the summers at the château
stops.date_confidence: attested for the property and the family's use of it; the year here stands for a childhood, not an event
stops.campa: The manor near the Rhône belongs to a great-aunt and then, from 1920, to his mother. Summers are spent here: a chapel where he was baptized, a park, a walled garden, roses. Biographers reading backward from Le Petit Prince find the prince's rose and the prince's garden in this ground and say so plainly; Saint-Exupéry himself never says it. The estate is put up for sale in 1931 and sold to the Lyon school board on 20 December 1932, after a last family Christmas. The childhood house is not lost the way houses are lost in books. It is sold, to a municipality, for money.
suggested_refs: The Château de Saint-Maurice-de-Rémens, Ain, sold to the Lyon school board 20 December 1932
sources: Curtis Cate, Antoine de Saint-Exupéry: His Life and Times (1970)

stops.name: Le Mans, the Jesuit college
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: After the father's death the family takes a house at 21 rue du Clos-Margot, and Antoine enters the Jesuit Collège Notre-Dame-de-Sainte-Croix. He is not a distinguished pupil. He draws in the margins, writes verse, and is remembered by his masters for a distracted stubbornness rather than for results. The Jesuits give him Latin and a habit of moral argument. Twenty-five years later the sentences of Terre des hommes still reason like a sermon and land like a report filed from a cockpit.
suggested_refs: Collège Notre-Dame-de-Sainte-Croix, Le Mans

stops.name: Fribourg, the Villa Saint-Jean
stops.date_confidence: attested for the school and the 1917 baccalauréat; the enrollment year is the biographers' range
stops.campa: The war sends the brothers across the Swiss border to the Villa Saint-Jean at Fribourg, a Marianist boarding school out of reach of the front. Antoine takes his baccalauréat here in 1917. The school is Catholic and comfortable, and its boys come from half of Europe. The two brothers are in it together. François is fifteen and Antoine seventeen, and by every account the younger is the steadier of the two. Their mother writes to both of them at the same address. It is the last school year in which Antoine de Saint-Exupéry has a brother.
suggested_refs: Villa Saint-Jean, Fribourg, Marianist boarding school of the war years

stops.name: Saint-Maurice-de-Rémens, the death of François
stops.date_confidence: contested: the summer of 1917 and the rheumatic fever are attested, but fr.wikipedia gives no place, en.wikipedia leaves the scene near Fribourg, and Schiff and Cate put the death at the family house on 10 July with Antoine at the bedside; the biographers are followed here
stops.campa: François dies in the summer of 1917 of rheumatic fever with pericarditis, aged fifteen. The standard biographies put the death at the family house of Saint-Maurice-de-Rémens on 10 July, with Antoine at the bedside; the encyclopedias give only the season, and one of them leaves the scene at Fribourg. What is not in dispute is what Antoine did with it. He writes the deathbed twice: once in Pilote de guerre, as a brother handing over an engine and a rifle in the tone of a man settling accounts, and once, readers have always said, as a boy who lies down in the sand and does not cry out.
suggested_refs: The deathbed scene of François de Saint-Exupéry as retold in Pilote de guerre (1942)

stops.name: Paris, the Navy refuses him twice
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He sits the entrance examination for the Naval Academy twice and fails twice. Instead he enrolls at the École des Beaux-Arts as an auditor in architecture, without a place and without money. Paris in 1919 is full of demobilized men barely older than the war they fought; he is younger still, an aristocrat's son with no profession and a talent for drawing small figures in the corners of paper. The Navy has refused him the sea. Nobody has yet mentioned the air, and the air is two years off.
suggested_refs: École des Beaux-Arts, Paris, architecture section, auditor 1919

segments.name: The Brevet Bought with His Own Money

stops.name: Strasbourg-Neuhof, the conscript pays for his lessons
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Called up in April 1921, he is posted to the 2e régiment d'aviation de chasse at Neuhof, outside Strasbourg, on the ground. English accounts turn this unit into a cavalry regiment of chasseurs; the French records do not. He pays for civilian flying lessons out of his own pocket, against his mother's wishes, and on 9 July 1921 he flies alone and takes the civil brevet. The transaction is exact: the army gives him an aerodrome and a uniform, and he buys the flying himself, in cash, before anyone has authorized it.
suggested_refs: The 2e régiment d'aviation de chasse at Neuhof, Strasbourg, and the civil brevet of 9 July 1921
sources: Curtis Cate, Antoine de Saint-Exupéry: His Life and Times (1970)

stops.name: Casablanca, Camp Cazes, the military brevet
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Assigned on 2 August 1921 to the 37e régiment d'aviation at Camp Cazes, he crosses to Morocco and finishes what he had bought in Strasbourg. On 23 December he is breveted a military pilot. The country under the wing is the first desert he sees from above: ochre, unmarked, legible only as a set of bearings between two coastal towns. He will keep coming back to it for twenty years, first with mail sacks, then with a broken Simoun and no water, and finally as the landscape a child walks out of in a book written on Long Island.
suggested_refs: Camp Cazes, Casablanca, base of the 37e régiment d'aviation

stops.name: Le Bourget, the fractured skull
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Posted to the 34e régiment d'aviation outside Paris, he crashes on 1 May 1923 and fractures his skull. The injury ends his military flying and puts him on the ground for three years: he sells trucks, works in a tile company's office, keeps writing in the evenings and showing the pages to nobody who matters. It is the first of the crashes and the least famous of them. He mends slowly and not completely. Then he goes back to aircraft, which is what he will do after every crash that follows this one.
stops.quote: Each man must look to himself to teach him the meaning of life. It is not something discovered: it is something molded.
stops.quote_source: Terre des hommes / Wind, Sand and Stars (1939), trans. Lewis Galantière
suggested_refs: Le Bourget aerodrome, 34e régiment d'aviation, the crash of 1 May 1923

stops.name: Paris, L'Aviateur in Le Navire d'Argent
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: The novella L'Aviateur appears in Le Navire d'Argent, a small Paris literary review, and is his first published fiction. It is about a pilot who dies in a crash. He is twenty-six, out of the army, unemployed in any serious sense, and has already found the subject he will keep: what a man in a cockpit owes to the ground, to the machine, and to the other men on the line. Within months the airmail company at Toulouse hires him and hands him the material by contract.
suggested_refs: L'Aviateur, in Le Navire d'Argent (Paris, 1926)

stops.name: Toulouse-Montaudran, Daurat and the royal grease
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Latécoère takes him on in October 1926 and sends him to Montaudran, the field the Toulouse to Dakar mail runs from. Operations are directed by Didier Daurat, who makes new pilots strip and clean engines before he lets them near the line, and who told Jean Mermoz that he needed bus drivers and not circus artists. Saint-Exupéry serves his grease under that man here, in Toulouse, three years before Buenos Aires. Rivière, the director in Vol de Nuit, is this man, and the novel is dedicated to him.
stops.quote: It seems that perfection is attained not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing more to take away.
stops.quote_source: Terre des hommes (1939), ch. III, 'L'Avion' ('The Tool'), trans. Lewis Galantière; French: 'Il semble que la perfection soit atteinte non quand il n'y a plus rien à ajouter, mais quand il n'y a plus rien à retrancher.'
suggested_refs: Toulouse-Montaudran, home field of Lignes Latécoère and the Compagnie Générale Aéropostale
Didier Daurat, Saint-Exupéry tel que je l'ai connu (Liège, 1954)

stops.name: Alicante, the Spanish legs of the line
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the route and its stopovers are documented, but no source names Saint-Exupéry at this field on a given date
stops.campa: The line runs down the Spanish coast in short hops, and new pilots are given these before they are trusted with anything harder. Alicante is a refuelling stop: a field, a windsock, a mechanic, a bed. The mail is the point and the pilot is the delivery mechanism, and the company's discipline holds that the sacks go through in any weather a man can survive. No document places Saint-Exupéry at this field on any particular day. The route is documented; the man on this leg of it is inferred from the roster of the line.
suggested_refs: The Aéropostale Spanish sector: Toulouse, Barcelona, Alicante, Málaga, Casablanca
sources: Standard Aéropostale route histories, cited generically in the research pool without a named title

stops.name: Agadir, the last field before the ransom country
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the sector is documented, the month is not
stops.campa: Agadir is the last Moroccan field before the line runs into a stretch of coast the company cannot police and the Spanish do not. South of here a forced landing means capture, and the tribes of the interior hold downed fliers for ransom as ordinary business. Pilots fly the sector in pairs when aircraft can be spared. The mail continues in either case. In his writing the line stops being a transport company on this leg. It becomes an order, with vows and a rate of attrition.
suggested_refs: The Aéropostale desert sector between Agadir and Cap Juby
sources: Standard Aéropostale route histories, cited generically in the research pool without a named title

stops.name: Cap Juby, chief of the fort
stops.date_confidence: attested for the posting; the month is the biographers' range
stops.campa: He is made chief of the stopover at Cap Juby, a Spanish fort on the Saharan coast with a wooden shed for the airline and almost nothing else beside it. For a year he lives between the garrison and the desert, negotiating in person with Sahrawi tribesmen for the release of fliers held for ransom, learning enough Arabic to bargain, writing at night. Courrier Sud is written here. France gives him the Légion d'honneur in 1930 for the negotiations. Six centuries earlier Ibn Battuta crossed this desert by salt caravan, moving goods the same way and for the same reason.
stops.quote: To be a man is, precisely, to be responsible. It is to feel shame at the sight of what seems to be unmerited misery. It is to take pride in a victory won by one's comrades. It is to feel, when setting one's stone, that one is contributing to the building of the world.
stops.quote_source: Terre des hommes / Wind, Sand and Stars (1939), ch. II, 'The Men', trans. Lewis Galantière
suggested_refs: The Aéropostale shed and Spanish fort at Cap Juby (Tarfaya), Spanish Sahara
sources: Curtis Cate, Antoine de Saint-Exupéry: His Life and Times (1970)

stops.name: Dakar, the southern anchor
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the terminus and its function are documented, the date is a placeholder within his Cap Juby years
stops.campa: Dakar is the southern anchor of the African line: the place where sacks flown down from Toulouse are handed onward toward the South Atlantic and the Brazilian coast. Aéropostale is building a system to move a letter from France to Argentina in days rather than weeks, and every field between Toulouse and here exists to serve that one number. Saint-Exupéry flies the sectors and inspects the fields. By the time he leaves Africa the company has handed him his two geographies, the desert and the sea.
suggested_refs: Dakar, African terminus of the Toulouse mail line and transfer point for the South Atlantic crossing
sources: Standard Aéropostale route histories, cited generically in the research pool without a named title

stops.name: Paris, Courrier Sud
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: Courrier Sud is published in 1929, drawn straight from the Casablanca to Dakar run and from Cap Juby. It sells modestly. The reviews treat it as a pilot's book by a pilot, which is exactly what it is. What it establishes is that the airmail company has produced a novelist who works from inside the cockpit rather than from the aerodrome fence, and that the discipline Daurat imposed at Montaudran can be written down as a moral system. Gallimard is watching. So is André Gide. The next book will not sell modestly.
suggested_refs: Courrier Sud (Paris, 1929), his first novel

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Galería Güemes and the directorship
stops.date_confidence: contested: fr.wikipedia has him joining Guillaumet in South America in September 1929, the geography lens dates the directorship to October 1929, and es.wikipedia's biography says 1928; the first firmly dated Argentine action is the inspection flight of 29 October
stops.campa: He sails for South America in the autumn of 1929 and takes up the post of Director de Explotación of Aeroposta Argentina, the Aéropostale subsidiary, with an apartment in the Galería Güemes off Florida street. The same October, Le Corbusier is lecturing in this city and flying over the delta of the Río de la Plata, and Victoria Ocampo is receiving him at San Isidro; fifteen months later she founds Sur. Nothing in the record puts the airline director and the review's founder in one room. They are working inside the same six blocks.
stops.quote: Even our misfortunes are a part of our belongings.
stops.quote_source: Vol de Nuit / Night Flight (1931), trans. Stuart Gilbert
suggested_refs: The Galería Güemes, Florida 165 / San Martín 170, Buenos Aires
Aeroposta Argentina company records naming him Director de Explotación

stops.name: Bahía Blanca, the inspection flights
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The line he is given to open runs south from Buenos Aires along a coast with almost nothing on it. Bahía Blanca is the last real town before the route enters that emptiness. From 29 October to 1 November 1929 he flies the final inspection runs himself, field by field, and the Buenos Aires to Comodoro Rivadavia service opens on the first of November. Fifty years earlier Julio Argentino Roca's campaign and the territorial law of 1884 had drawn the administrative lines on this ground that the mail plane now crosses in an afternoon.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires to Bahía Blanca to Comodoro Rivadavia mail line, inaugurated 1 November 1929

stops.name: Comodoro Rivadavia, the wind and the night mail
stops.date_confidence: attested for the field and the line's opening; the identification of this town with the atmosphere of Vol de Nuit is a reader's tradition, not a claim of the novel
stops.campa: An oil town on a Patagonian shore where the wind does not stop. The field here is the southern terminus of the new line, and the weather that makes it notorious among pilots is the weather Vol de Nuit is made of: night, cyclone, radio silence, a man above cloud he cannot get under. The novel names no real town and no source puts this one in it. Aimé Tschiffely had ridden out of these provinces four years earlier on criollo horses bred on the Chubut steppe, covering the same distances at four kilometres an hour.
stops.quote: La femme du pilote, réveillée par le téléphone, regarda son mari et pensa : Je le laisse dormir encore un peu.
stops.quote_source: Vol de Nuit (1931), ch. X, p. 91
suggested_refs: The Aeroposta Argentina field at Comodoro Rivadavia, southern terminus of the 1929 line

stops.name: Río Gallegos, the line stops here
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: The line pushes further south through 1930 and reaches Río Gallegos in March, near the bottom of the Argentine mainland, within sight of the approaches to the Strait of Magellan. It goes no further in his time. There is no Chilean service and no Punta Arenas leg, whatever later accounts assert; Río Grande comes in September 1935, four years after he has gone. What he built and inspected is a corridor of small fields down a coast where engine failure is not an incident but a sentence.
suggested_refs: The Aeroposta Argentina southern line to Río Gallegos, March 1930

stops.name: Mendoza, the gate of the cordillera
stops.date_confidence: attested for the route and his writing about it; his own presence in the city is inferred from the Guillaumet search
stops.campa: Mendoza sits at the gate of the cordillera, staging point for the crossing to Chile that Jean Mermoz opened and that kills pilots in ordinary weather. Saint-Exupéry writes about these crossings with the flat admiration of a man who knows the numbers: the passes, the ceilings, a Potez 25's rate of climb measured against a mountain wall. The company's answer to the Andes is the same as its answer to the Sahara. The mail goes, and the men who carry it accept in advance what carrying it may cost them.
stops.quote: If, when Mermoz plunged into the Chilean Andes with victory in his heart, you had protested to him that no merchant's letter could possibly be worth risking one's life for, Mermoz would have laughed in your face.
stops.quote_source: Terre des hommes / Wind, Sand and Stars (1939), ch. IX, trans. Lewis Galantière
suggested_refs: The Aéropostale Andes crossing from Mendoza to Santiago, opened by Jean Mermoz

stops.name: The Andes, Guillaumet walks out
stops.date_confidence: attested for the crash and the survival; the coordinate is the Laguna Diamante sector by reconstruction, since no source fixes the crash point
stops.campa: On 13 June 1930 Henri Guillaumet, his closest friend on the line, goes down in a Potez 25 in the cordillera on his ninety-second crossing. Saint-Exupéry flies search patterns over the peaks for days and finds nothing. On the nineteenth Guillaumet walks out alive, having crossed three passes on foot in a week, and says the sentence Saint-Exupéry will carry into Terre des hommes and never improve on. The exact crash point is not fixed in any reachable source. The walk out of it is fixed in a book that has never gone out of print.
stops.quote: What I have done, I swear to you, no animal would have done.
stops.quote_source: Henri Guillaumet to Saint-Exupéry, Andes, June 1930, recounted in Terre des hommes (1939)
suggested_refs: Guillaumet's Potez 25 crash and seven-day walk out of the Andes, June 1930

segments.name: Nice, Agay, and the Night Flight

stops.name: Nice, the civil marriage to Consuelo
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He marries Consuelo Suncín Sandoval, a Salvadoran writer and artist and twice a widow, in a civil ceremony at Nice on 22 April 1931. They had met in Buenos Aires while he was running the airline. The marriage will be the least navigable thing in his life: separations, returns, letters posted from three continents, and a rose in a book that everyone including Consuelo read as herself. He is thirty. He has written the novel that will make him famous and has not yet published it.
suggested_refs: Consuelo Suncín de Sandoval, Salvadoran writer, and her memoir The Tale of the Rose

stops.name: Agay, the wedding at his sister's house
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The religious wedding follows the next day at Agay, on the coast near Saint-Raphaël, at the property belonging to his sister Gabrielle's family. The house becomes the address he comes back to between postings, records, crashes, and wars: the one place in France that stays his through all of it. He will fly over this coast for the last time in July 1944, outbound from Corsica toward the Rhône, and go into the sea about a hundred and thirty kilometres west of the church he was married in.
suggested_refs: The Agay estate near Saint-Raphaël, home of his sister Gabrielle's family

stops.name: Paris, Vol de Nuit and the Prix Femina
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Gallimard publishes Vol de Nuit on 19 September 1931 with a preface by André Gide, and it takes the Prix Femina the same year. The novel is set on the Patagonian night mail he ran, and its director Rivière, who spends men because the service must not stop, is Didier Daurat of Toulouse. The book makes him famous the way a prize makes a man famous, quickly and in one country. Hollywood buys it inside two years. He is a working airline manager who has just become a literary property.
suggested_refs: Vol de nuit (Gallimard, 1931), preface by André Gide, Prix Femina 1931

stops.name: The Libyan Desert, the Simoun goes in
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the aircraft, and the four days; the coordinate is the Wadi Natrun region only, since no source records where the aeroplane struck and the research pool's own lenses give three different values
stops.campa: Flying a Caudron C-630 Simoun on a Paris to Saigon speed attempt, he and his mechanic André Prévot go into the ground in the Libyan Desert of Egypt, in the Wadi Natrun country northwest of Cairo, on 30 December 1935. They walk for four days on almost no water, hallucinating toward the end, and are found by a Bedouin on a camel who gives them the rehydration a desert man knows how to give. No source records where the aeroplane hit. The desert in the book he writes afterwards has no coordinates either.
stops.quote: What makes the desert beautiful is that it hides, somewhere, a well.
stops.quote_source: Le Petit Prince / The Little Prince (1943), trans. Katherine Woods, ch. XXIV; often miscited to Terre des hommes
suggested_refs: The Caudron C-630 Simoun and the Paris to Saigon raid of December 1935

stops.name: Cairo, the two men come out of the sand
stops.date_confidence: attested to the first days of January 1936
stops.campa: They reach Cairo in the first days of 1936, alive, burned to the bone, and famous for a week. The record is lost and the aircraft is scrap. What he has instead is four days of material that will be paid out twice: as reportage inside Terre des hommes, and seven years later as the opening situation of a children's book, where a pilot sits down in the sand a thousand miles from anywhere and a small voice asks him to draw a sheep. He is thirty-five, and he has now been down in the desert as the man who had to be fetched.
suggested_refs: Cairo, end of the December 1935 desert ordeal

stops.name: Guatemala City, La Aurora, the takeoff that fails
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On 15 February 1938 he attempts the New York to Punta Arenas distance record and crashes on takeoff at La Aurora field in Guatemala City, badly enough that the injuries never entirely leave him. Punta Arenas is a place he never reaches by air in any capacity: the Aeroposta line he once directed stopped well short of it, at Río Gallegos. He convalesces for months. Terre des hommes is assembled during that recovery, out of the Sahara, the Andes, Cap Juby, and a decade on the line.
suggested_refs: La Aurora airfield, Guatemala City, crash of 15 February 1938

stops.name: Paris, Terre des hommes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: Terre des hommes appears in February 1939, and Reynal and Hitchcock publish Wind, Sand and Stars in New York the same year, dedicated to Guillaumet. It takes the Grand Prix du roman de l'Académie française in France and the National Book Award in the United States. It is not a novel and not quite a memoir: it is a working pilot's account of what the trade taught him about other men, assembled from the fields of two continents. Six months after publication, France is at war.
stops.quote: No man can draw a free breath who does not share with other men a common and disinterested ideal. Life has taught us that love does not consist in gazing at each other but in looking outward together in the same direction.
stops.quote_source: Terre des hommes / Wind, Sand and Stars (1939), ch. IX, trans. Lewis Galantière
suggested_refs: Terre des hommes (Gallimard, 1939) and Wind, Sand and Stars (Reynal and Hitchcock, 1939)

stops.name: Arras, the reconnaissance over the collapse
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the sources date his II/33 reconnaissance flying to 1940, and the Arras mission is dated from Pilote de guerre rather than from a squadron document
stops.campa: He flies reconnaissance in a Bloch MB.174 with Groupe de reconnaissance II/33 through the collapse of 1940, over roads full of people walking south and towns burning behind them. The mission over Arras becomes Pilote de guerre: a low run through flak in an aircraft that cannot shoot back, flown for photographs that will be delivered to a command structure which has stopped existing. He is thirty-nine and the oldest man in the crew room by the better part of a decade.
stops.quote: A rock pile ceases to be a rock pile the moment a single man contemplates it, bearing within him the image of a cathedral.
stops.quote_source: Pilote de guerre / Flight to Arras (1942), trans. Lewis Galantière
suggested_refs: Groupe de reconnaissance II/33 and the Bloch MB.174 sorties of May and June 1940

stops.name: Estoril, the Hotel Palácio and the waiting
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: After the armistice he leaves France and waits out the paperwork at the Hotel Palácio in Estoril, from 28 November to 20 December 1940. The hotel is full of people in the same condition: visas, wired money, a casino across the road, the Atlantic behind it. Guillaumet had been shot down over the Mediterranean the day before he arrived here, flying a Farman airliner to Syria. Saint-Exupéry leaves Europe having lost the man he flew the Andes and the Sahara alongside, and having lost the country in the same season.
suggested_refs: The Hotel Palácio, Estoril, transit point for refugees from occupied Europe

stops.name: New York, the Siboney docks
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The S.S. Siboney lands him in New York on the last day of 1940. He speaks almost no English and will not learn it. The French exile community in the city is at war with itself over de Gaulle, over Vichy, over who is entitled to speak for a country that has stopped existing on schedule; he refuses to join a faction and is attacked from every direction for the refusal. He is the most famous French writer in America and he is not comfortable in any room he is invited into.
suggested_refs: The S.S. Siboney, arrival at New York 31 December 1940

stops.name: New York, Central Park South and the Astor luncheon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the award and the date; the apartments are attested without exact dates
stops.campa: He takes apartments on Central Park South and later on Beekman Place, and on 14 January 1941 he is given the National Book Award for Wind, Sand and Stars at a luncheon at the Hotel Astor. He writes Pilote de guerre in this city, and Lettre à un otage, in which he sets down what he owes his dead. The exile runs twenty-seven months. He spends them arguing for a France that will be put back together by men who fly, and petitioning anyone who will hear him to let him fly again.
stops.quote: Du pilote Guillaumet, le dernier ami que j'ai perdu et qui s'est fait abattre en service postal aérien, mon Dieu ! J'ai accepté de porter le deuil.
suggested_refs: Saint-Exupéry's New York apartments on Central Park South and Beekman Place
The National Book Award luncheon at the Hotel Astor, 14 January 1941

stops.name: Quebec City, the lecture tour
stops.date_confidence: attested to May and June 1942
stops.campa: A lecture tour takes him to French Canada in May and June 1942, and he stays in Quebec City on the rue Sainte-Geneviève with the family of the philosopher Charles De Koninck. He is ill for part of it and held up at the border by paperwork on the way back. The tour is the last time he stands on a stage as a public man rather than waiting on a field as a pilot without a posting. He talks about France to people who have kept a version of it in their mouths for three hundred years.
suggested_refs: The De Koninck house on rue Sainte-Geneviève, Quebec City

stops.name: Asharoken, the Bevin House and the manuscript
stops.date_confidence: attested for the completion of the manuscript in October 1942; en.wikipedia dates the rental to 'late 1942'
stops.campa: Late in 1942 he rents the Bevin House, a white clapboard mansion on Long Island Sound at Asharoken, and finishes Le Petit Prince there in October, writing at night and painting the watercolours himself. He had asked for a hut and been given twenty-two rooms. The book is a desert, a crashed aeroplane, a mechanic's problem with a water supply, and a child who is not a child. One of the sketches made in this house will be printed on the French fifty-franc note from 1993 to 2002.
stops.quote: Grown-ups never understand anything by themselves, and it is tiresome for children to be always and forever explaining things to them.
stops.quote_source: Le Petit Prince / The Little Prince (1943), trans. Katherine Woods
suggested_refs: The Delamater-Bevin Mansion, Asharoken, Long Island
The French 50-franc note of 1993, carrying a Saint-Exupéry sketch

stops.name: New York, Le Petit Prince is published
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1943; the day is the publisher's, carried by en.wikipedia
stops.campa: Reynal and Hitchcock publish Le Petit Prince in April 1943, in English and in French at once, in New York, in wartime, in a country where the author cannot read his own reviews. It is dedicated to Léon Werth, when he was a little boy. By the counts of the next eighty years it will be translated into some six hundred languages and dialects and sold about a hundred and forty million times, second only to the Bible among translated books. He leaves the continent the same month it appears.
stops.quote: It is only with the heart that one can see rightly; what is essential is invisible to the eye.
stops.quote_source: Le Petit Prince / The Little Prince (1943), trans. Katherine Woods
suggested_refs: Le Petit Prince (Reynal and Hitchcock, New York, April 1943), first edition in English and French

stops.name: Algiers, before General Giraud
stops.date_confidence: attested: departure from North America in April 1943 per en.wikipedia, presentation to Giraud on 5 May 1943 per fr.wikipedia
stops.campa: He sails with an American military convoy in April 1943 and presents himself in Algiers to General Giraud on 5 May. He is forty-two, eight years over the age limit for a reconnaissance pilot, and carries a body broken at Le Bourget, in the Libyan Desert, and at Guatemala City. He petitions without stopping until an exemption is granted, and it is granted at the level of General Eisenhower. Groupe de reconnaissance 2/33, called Savoie, takes him back and puts him on Lightnings he has to learn from a manual he cannot read.
stops.quote: For the first time in the history of the world, your young men are dying in a war that, despite all its horrors, is for them an experience of love.
stops.quote_source: 'Letter to an American' (1944), published in Life magazine
suggested_refs: Groupe de reconnaissance 2/33 'Savoie' and the Eisenhower age exemption

stops.name: Borgo-Poretta, Corsica, the last field
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On 17 July 1944 the group moves to Borgo-Poretta, outside Bastia in Corsica, for the reconnaissance flights that will go ahead of the Allied landings in Provence. The aircraft is a Lockheed F-5B, a P-38 Lightning stripped of its guns and fitted with cameras: unarmed, fast, flown alone and high over a coast held by fighters. He is by a distance the oldest pilot on the field, the worst of them at paperwork, and the only one whose books are in the mess.
suggested_refs: Borgo-Poretta airfield, Bastia, Corsica, base of GR 2/33 in July 1944

stops.name: Off Riou Island, the flight that does not return
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the loss; the takeoff hour is contested, fr.wikipedia giving 08:25 and en.wikipedia 08:45, with both agreeing it was full daylight
stops.campa: He takes off from Borgo on the morning of 31 July 1944 for a photographic run over the Rhône valley, alone, in the unarmed F-5B serial 42-68223. The French sources put the wheels up at 08:25 and the English at 08:45; both agree it was full daylight, hours after sunrise. He does not come back, and no one sees him go down. The squadron waits for the fuel to run out on paper and then writes him off. He is forty-four, and the water he goes into is a hundred and thirty kilometres west of the coast he was married on.
stops.quote: Your task is not to foresee the future, but to enable it.
stops.quote_source: Citadelle / The Wisdom of the Sands (1948, posthumous), trans. Stuart Gilbert
suggested_refs: Lockheed F-5B-1-LO serial 42-68223, the aircraft of 31 July 1944

stops.name: Paris, the inscription in the Panthéon
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the wall inscription is attested, but the November 1967 legislative act rests on en.wikipedia alone and is uncorroborated in French sources, which do not list him among those transferred to the Panthéon
stops.campa: An inscription is cut on a wall of the Panthéon: to the memory of Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, poet, novelist, aviator, lost in the course of an aerial reconnaissance mission on 31 July 1944. He had been declared mort pour la France in 1945. He is not buried here and he was never transferred here; the French lists of the pantheonized do not carry his name, and the date usually given for the act rests on a single encyclopedia. The nation's crypt holds one sentence about him and nothing underneath it.
suggested_refs: The commemorative wall inscription to Saint-Exupéry in the Panthéon, Paris
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Panthéon' (list of transfers, consulted as a negative)

stops.name: Marseille, the bracelet in the net
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1998; the day is carried by fr.wikipedia
stops.campa: On 7 September 1998 a fisherman working east of the Riou archipelago brings up a silver identity bracelet in his net, engraved with three names: Saint-Exupéry, Consuelo, and Reynal and Hitchcock, the New York house that published the Little Prince. It is the first physical trace of the loss in fifty-four years, and it fixes a search area. The bracelet had been in the water, within a few miles of a shipping lane, for the length of two generations. Everything found afterwards is found because a net closed on a piece of jewellery by accident.
suggested_refs: The silver identity bracelet recovered off Marseille, September 1998

stops.name: Off Riou, the wreck on the seabed
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 2000
stops.campa: In May 2000 a diver locates aircraft debris on the seabed off the northeast face of the Île de Riou, in water clear enough to photograph. It is a Lockheed P-38. The French state then takes two years to authorize a salvage, and the site sits under guard and under argument while the authorization is drafted. The wreck has been there since 1944 and can wait; the divers who found it are less patient than the wreck. No human remains are found at the site, then or at any point afterwards.
suggested_refs: The P-38 debris field off the northeast face of the Île de Riou, located May 2000

stops.name: Lyon, the airport takes his name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 2000; the day here is his birthday, used as a placeholder because the renaming date is not given in the sources
stops.campa: In 2000 the international airport of his native city is renamed Aéroport Lyon-Saint-Exupéry, and the man who spent his working life as an employee of a mail contract becomes a place where aircraft land. An asteroid in the outer main belt already carries his name, cited in July 1987 and chosen for the obvious reason: the prince in the book lives on one. The child in that book leaves his body behind in the sand because it is too heavy to carry. Nothing of the pilot was ever brought up out of the water.
suggested_refs: Aéroport Lyon-Saint-Exupéry, renamed 2000
Asteroid 2578 Saint-Exupéry, naming citation 11 July 1987

stops.name: Off Riou, the raising and the German claim
stops.date_confidence: contested: fr.wikipedia dates the lift to 1 to 3 September 2003, en.wikipedia to October 2003; the formal identification in 2004 is attested
stops.campa: The main wreckage is raised in 2003, and the sources cannot agree on the month: the French date the lift to the first three days of September, the English to October. In 2004 the aircraft is formally identified from its airframe serial number, 42-68223. It is his. Four years later a former Luftwaffe pilot, Horst Rippert, says publicly that he shot down a Lightning over this water that day, in a Messerschmitt, without knowing at the time whom he had hit. He offers no material proof, and the radio records do not carry him.
suggested_refs: The 2003 salvage and the 2004 identification of airframe 42-68223
Horst Rippert's 2008 statement, made without material proof
